The Problem: Your AI Keeps Making the Same Mistakes

Time: ~30-40 minutes | Prerequisites: Basic Python, curiosity
You're pair programming with an AI assistant. It suggests a pattern. You reject it—that's not how we do things here. Five minutes later, it suggests the same thing. Sound familiar? The AI isn't stupid. It's stuck. It has no mechanism to learn from your corrections. Every session starts fresh, repeating the same mistakes you've already flagged. What if it could learn? Not by fine-tuning a massive model. Something simpler: track which rules help, which don't, and adapt. A lightweight learning loop that runs on top of the AI. That's what we're building. And the algorithm that makes it work—Thompson Sampling—is one of the most elegant ideas in machine learning. By the end of this notebook, you'll:
  • Understand why "just pick the best one" fails
  • See uncertainty as a feature, not a bug
  • Build a working bandit that learns from feedback
  • Watch it outperform both random and greedy strategies
Let's go.

Layer 1: The Explore-Exploit Trap

The Restaurant Analogy

You're in a new city for 10 days. There are 3 restaurants near your hotel:
  • Restaurant A: You tried it once. Pretty good (7/10).
  • Restaurant B: Never tried it. Could be amazing. Could be terrible.
  • Restaurant C: Never tried it either.
Where do you eat tonight? Option 1: Exploit — Go back to A. You know it's decent. Safe bet. Option 2: Explore — Try B or C. Higher variance, but you might find something better. Here's the trap:
  • Pure exploitation: You eat at A every night. Maybe B was a 9/10. You'll never know.
  • Pure exploration: You rotate randomly. Even after discovering B is great, you keep wasting nights on mediocre C.
Neither extreme is optimal. The best strategy? Explore intelligently. Try new things when you're uncertain. Stick with winners once you're confident. Let your uncertainty guide you.

Layer 2: Code + Viz — The Cost of Bad Strategies

Let's make this concrete. We'll simulate 3 "arms" (restaurants, rules, whatever) with hidden success probabilities. Then we'll compare strategies.

Problem 1: Set Up the Simulation

We have 3 arms with true (hidden) probabilities of success:
  • Arm 0: 30% chance of reward
  • Arm 1: 50% chance of reward
  • Arm 2: 70% chance of reward ← the best one
Your task: Create a function that "pulls" an arm and returns 1 (success) or 0 (failure) based on its true probability.

Problem 2: Implement Competing Strategies

Let's implement three strategies and race them:
  1. Random: Pick an arm uniformly at random each time
  2. Greedy: Always pick the arm with the highest observed success rate
  3. Epsilon-Greedy: Usually greedy, but explore randomly 10% of the time
We'll track cumulative regret: how much reward we lost compared to always picking the best arm.
Let's Race Them

What you're seeing:
  • Random (blue): Linear regret. It never learns. ~40% of pulls go to suboptimal arms forever.
  • Greedy (orange): Might get lucky and find the best arm early. But often locks onto a mediocre arm and never escapes. High variance across runs.
  • ε-Greedy (green): Better! The 10% exploration prevents complete lock-in. But it keeps exploring at 10% even after it knows the answer. Wasteful.
None of these are great. We need something smarter.

Layer 1: Uncertainty to the Rescue

The Key Insight

What if instead of tracking just "arm 2 succeeded 7 out of 10 times", we tracked our full uncertainty about arm 2's true probability? After 7 successes and 3 failures, we're pretty sure arm 2 is good. But after 1 success and 0 failures? We have almost no idea. Enter the Beta distribution. The Beta distribution is a probability distribution over probabilities. It answers: "Given what I've observed, what's my belief about the true success rate?" Two parameters:
  • α (alpha): pseudo-count of successes (starts at 1)
  • β (beta): pseudo-count of failures (starts at 1)
After observing s successes and f failures:
  • α = 1 + s
  • β = 1 + f
The shape of Beta(α, β) is your uncertainty.

Layer 2: Code + Viz — The Beta Distribution

Problem 3: Visualize Uncertainty

Let's see what Beta distributions look like as we gather evidence.

What you're seeing:
  1. Beta(1,1): Uniform—we have no idea. Could be 0.1, could be 0.9.
  2. Beta(2,2): After one success and one failure, we think it's around 0.5, but very uncertain.
  3. Beta(8,4): After 10 observations (7 wins), we're centering on ~0.7 with less spread.
  4. Beta(71,31): After 100 observations, we're confident. The distribution is tight.
This is Bayesian inference in action. Your uncertainty is a first-class citizen, not a nuisance.

Layer 1: Thompson Sampling

The Algorithm

Here's the beautiful insight: instead of computing complex exploration bonuses, just sample your uncertainty. Thompson Sampling:
  1. For each arm, sample a value from its Beta distribution
  2. Pick the arm with the highest sampled value
  3. Pull it, observe reward, update the Beta parameters
  4. Repeat
That's it. That's the whole algorithm. Why it works:
  • Arms you're uncertain about have wide distributions → sometimes sample high → get explored
  • Arms you're confident about have narrow distributions → sample near their mean
  • As you learn, exploitation naturally dominates—without an explicit schedule
Exploration falls out of the math. You don't tune an ε. You don't decay anything. It just works.

Layer 2: Code + Viz — Thompson Sampling

Problem 4: Implement Thompson Sampling
The Showdown

Thompson Sampling (dark green) crushes it. It explores early (high variance in the curves), then converges to near-zero regret growth once it's confident arm 2 is best. No tuning required. This is what buildlog uses to select which rules to surface. Rules that help get reinforced. Rules that don't get deprioritized. Automatically.

Layer 2: Watch It Learn

Problem 5: Visualize the Learning Process

Let's watch Thompson Sampling's beliefs evolve over time.

Watch the beliefs sharpen:
  • Round 0: All three arms have identical flat priors (no data yet)
  • Round 10-30: Beliefs start separating as we gather observations
  • Round 70+: Arm 2 (green) is clearly recognized as best—its distribution is tight around 0.7
  • Round 199: All three distributions are tight around their true values
The dotted vertical lines are the true probabilities. Notice how the beliefs converge toward them.

Exercises

Try these to deepen your understanding.

Exercise 1: Change the Priors

What if arm 2 started with a "reputation"—say, a prior of Beta(5, 1) instead of Beta(1, 1)? This is called a boosted prior. Modify thompson_sampling_strategy to accept initial priors. Hint: This is how buildlog gives "seed rules" (expert-curated axioms) a head start.

Exercise 2: Non-Stationary Environment

What if the true probabilities change halfway through? (Arm 1 becomes best after round 250.) Run a simulation where TRUE_PROBS shifts at round 250. How does Thompson Sampling handle it? What about ε-Greedy? Hint: Thompson Sampling adapts naturally because it never stops exploring—just explores less.

Exercise 3: More Arms

Add a 4th arm with true probability 0.65 (close to arm 2's 0.70). How does Thompson Sampling handle near-ties? Does regret increase? Hint: It should—distinguishing similar arms requires more exploration.

What You Just Built

You implemented Thompson Sampling, one of the most elegant algorithms in machine learning. Key takeaways:
  1. Exploit vs Explore is a false dichotomy. Smart algorithms do both, weighted by uncertainty.
  2. Uncertainty is a feature. The Beta distribution encodes what you don't know.
  3. Sampling beats tuning. No ε to set. No decay schedule. Just sample your beliefs.
  4. It's practical. This exact algorithm powers buildlog's rule selection.

What's Next

In 01-uncertainty-as-superpower, we'll go deeper on the Beta distribution:
  • Why Beta(1,1) is the "I have no idea" prior
  • How α and β relate to sample size and confidence
  • Conjugate priors and why Bayesians love them
For now: you have a working bandit. Play with the exercises. Break things. Learn. → 01-uncertainty-as-superpower.py
